rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their dreadful fate followed indifference to God's reminder and neglect of the Messenger's teachings; God appointed evil leaders who deceived them until promised punishment arrived.
rows.anchor: they showed indifference to the reminder of God and instead of paying head to the teachings of His messenger did not give them due importance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointment of evil companions follows the established divine practice that one who disregards God's remembrance receives a devil as companion; devils among jinn and humans persist until punishment comes.
rows.anchor: he who becomes indifferent to the remembrance of God, We depute a devil on him who becomes his companion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The devils embellish a nation's past and present so it sees no faults in its actions, character, beliefs, or ideas and follows their path despite prophetic and righteous admonition.
rows.anchor: they are not able to see any shortcoming in their deeds and character, beliefs and ideology

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened divine decree is the punishment announced to nations that rejected their messengers, which came to each such nation.
rows.anchor: the threat of God’s punishment sounded by God to nations which rejected their respective messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the verse says disbelievers generally, textual clues identify the Quraysh leaders who ruled Arabia's idolaters; they told their men to drown out Qur'an recitation and stop people listening.
rows.anchor: they refer to the leaders among disbelievers who reigned on the idolaters of Arabia

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will inflict painful torment and expose the worst consequences of their deeds, which they cannot assess fully in this life.
rows.anchor: the Almighty will make them taste a painful torment, and bring before them the most horrible aspect of their deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh leaders directed their men to drown out Qur’anic recitation, prevent others from listening, and overpower Muhammad’s voice with noise.
rows.anchor: they should hoot and yell at it to create discord and pandemonium

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deeds affect others and may multiply greatly: a small virtue can grow like a mountain, and vice can likewise grow beyond its apparent size.
rows.anchor: at times a small virtue multiplies and becomes as large as a mountain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deeds can affect others and multiply in consequence: Cain shares responsibility for later unjust murders because he initiated that crime; full measure of sin appears only at Judgment.
rows.anchor: whenever this kind of murder takes place it adds to the sin of Cain as he is partly responsible for it by initiating it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's reference to the worst punishment points to leaders' inability to gauge how much sin they accrue by obstructing Qur'an and creating confusion around it.
rows.anchor: It is only when all the results come before them that they will be able to know the extent of loss

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative refers to the previously described horrible fate; the enemies of God are Quraysh leaders who used thugs to suppress Qur'an, and their result is Hell and permanent abode for denying and obstructing revelation.
rows.anchor: the leaders of the Quraysh who through their rouges and ruffians were after subduing the call of the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun “the Fire” stands as a complete sentence with its subject omitted to emphasize the predicate: the result is Hell.
rows.anchor: In order to stress the enunciative ( khabar) the inchoative ( mubatadā’) has been suppressed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the disbelievers are named generally, context identifies the masses led astray by leaders; when they see the outcome, they will ask to trample those leaders and their jinn accomplices.
rows.anchor: they refer to the masses that were lured and led astray by their leaders

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masses want to trample their leaders to teach them a lesson for arrogance and abuse of power and thereby soothe themselves.
rows.anchor: teach them a lesson for their arrogance and misuse of power and thereby pacify themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing opponents' Judgment, the passage turns to those who accepted Muhammad's preaching and remained devoted and steadfast despite opposition; before judgment, angels comfort them and announce that their trial is over and Paradise awaits.
rows.anchor: angels will visit these people to please and comfort them; they will assure them that their time of trial is now over

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Devils accompanied disbelievers toward Hell, while angels accompanied believers in both worldly life and the next; Paradise grants believers everything they desire and ask for.
rows.anchor: angels remained the companions of the believers in the previous world and in this one

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels also remain with believers in this life, urging virtue and strengthening them through hardship; those who hand themselves over to Satan lose this support.
rows.anchor: they induce them towards virtue and also encourage and strengthen them in the hardships they face

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word nazul means the initial meal or feast offered to a guest, so Paradise's present favour is God's first act of hospitality; what follows is known only to God.
rows.anchor: refers to the initial meal and feast given to a guest

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse reassures the Prophet and censures opponents who had claimed in 41:5 that their hearts, ears, and a veil blocked his message; their refusal and disruption are their fault, not his or the message's.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) is being told that if these people are not listening to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's message is God's oneness and worship, while his own righteous conduct matches his call and testifies that he seeks virtue and justice rather than disorder.
rows.anchor: the message of the Prophet (sws) is that of tawḥīd of God and to worship Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His declaration that he is obedient to his Lord shows he seeks everyone's submission to God, not political dominance; Islam is the universe's natural religion and the faith Abraham preached, whom the Ishmaelites claim.
rows.anchor: he is not after establishing his political dominance over people; in fact, he wants to make everyone obedient to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If opponents persist despite these clear signs, the Prophet should leave their case to God, who alone can remove the coverings over their hearts.
rows.anchor: None except God can lift the covers that have enveloped their hearts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good and bad conduct produce sharply different effects and consequences for both the Hereafter and the goals of preaching.
rows.anchor: There is a world of difference between the effect and consequences of both

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although equal retaliation is permitted, forgiveness and patience are better in God's sight and more effective for preaching and reform.
rows.anchor: though it is permitted to a person to exact an equal revenge for an excess committed against him, yet forgiveness and showing patience is even better

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an 16:125–126 calls for wise, kindly, best-mannered preaching and allows proportionate retaliation while naming patience the better course.
rows.anchor: And if you exercise patience, then this is the best way for the patient.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience and forgiveness are the better response while truth is still being conclusively conveyed; after rejection and active efforts to destroy believers and their message, taking opponents to task can become better or necessary.
rows.anchor: the believers are directed to adopt this behaviour until the truth is conclusively conveyed to their opponents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccans urged to forgive in this verse were later punished by the Companions at God's direction once the truth had been conclusively conveyed.
rows.anchor: the very people of Makkah with whom the Almighty urged the Prophet (sws) and his companions to adopt the attitude of forgiveness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The enemy's change into a close friend reflects human nature: even one initially moved by hostility can be touched by a person's persistent wish for their good despite mistreatment.
rows.anchor: When people whose nature has not been perverted see that so anxious is a person in wishing well for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Magnanimous conduct turns some opponents' hostility into affection; Muhammad's character was a leading force in his preaching, winning sincere companions from those with decency, while hardened hearts remained unmoved.
rows.anchor: the most effective factor in the preaching mission of Mu ḥammad (sws) was this aspect of his character

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun “it” has no stated antecedent and refers to the wisdom commanded in the previous verse; this unexpressed-reference construction is common in Arabic.
rows.anchor: it refers to the wisdom which the previous verse instructs Muslims to adopt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wisdom of answering evil with better conduct is attainable only by the patient; it is a profound, lasting treasure, so people should cultivate patience and strive to acquire it.
rows.anchor: this wisdom can be attained only by those who have the trait of patience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When opponents' mischief or Satan's suggestions stir feelings against wisdom, the remedy is to seek God's refuge sincerely rather than follow emotion; God hears and sees, grants refuge, and prevents Satan from prevailing.
rows.anchor: If a person instead being lured away by his emotions sincerely seeks God’s refuge, he will be definitely granted it by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Section IV resumes the sūrah's opening arguments for God's oneness and the Hereafter from the world around us, warns those who mislead others, and identifies the Qur'an as God's revelation.
rows.anchor: the arguments which were presented in the beginning of the sūrah to substantiate the beliefs of tawḥīd and the Hereafter are further explained

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Denying the Qur'an harms only its deniers and hastens their destruction; its revelation was a great favour to Ishmaelites and Israelites, and after truth has been fully conveyed their fate is deserved, not unjust.
rows.anchor: a great favour to both the Ishmaelites and the Israelites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each person alone bears the outcome of his deeds; God produces results according to their nature and is not unjust in the slightest, a principle also discussed in 45:15.
rows.anchor: God does not want that people be seized by Him if the truth has not been conclusively conveyed to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, negating an exaggerated expression intensifies the negation; here the meaning is that God is not unjust to His people in any degree.
rows.anchor: when there is a negation of an exaggeration, then its purpose is to create exaggeration in the negation itself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section warns that denying the Day because its arrival time is unknown is no prudence, then laments those demanding punishment despite God's respite for repentance; if seized, they would plead at length.
rows.anchor: denying a fact merely because its time of arrival cannot be divulged is no prudence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah closes by warning Qur'an-deniers that signs confirming its truth will soon appear in the world and within themselves, beyond denial.
rows.anchor: soon signs of its veracity will appear in the world around them and in that within them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt complements Sūrah Qāf: after Qāf answered doubts about resurrection, this sūrah validates both warning and reward and punishment; its theme is that the warning is true and recompense certain.
rows.anchor: This sūrah is the counterpart of Sūrah Qāf the previous sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah addresses Quraysh rejecters using signs within and around people, and concludes by assuring the Prophet as the previous sūrah did.
rows.anchor: The sūrah is addressed to the rejecters of the Quraysh, and the arguments are based on the reasoning found in the world within man and that around him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–14 use winds and striped clouds to rebuke mockers asking when Judgment will come, affirm that doom is certain, and say those demanding its arrival will be told to taste what they sought.
rows.anchor: ignorant people who make fun of the Day of reward and punishment by mockingly questioning about its time of arrival are severely reprimanded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those absorbed in heedlessness and wild conjecture are the ones who have lost their senses and dare to doubt the certainty of the warning.
rows.anchor: Only those who have lost their senses are daring to doubt their certainty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In contrast, the righteous fear Judgment, sleep little at night, seek forgiveness before dawn, and give the deprived a share of their wealth.
rows.anchor: who slept but little at night and in the early hours of dawn sought their Lord’s forgiveness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signs in the heavens, earth, and human soul attest to Judgment; an oath affirms that recreating humanity is as easy for God as uttering a word.
rows.anchor: The signs in the heavens and the earth, as well as in the human soul, which testify to the Day of Judgement are alluded to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The histories of Abraham and Lot provide further evidence: the angels who brought Abraham glad tidings brought punishment to Lot's people, while Lot and believers were saved; the preserved city ruins warn the God-fearing.
rows.anchor: The same angels who had brought glad tidings for Abraham (sws) that he

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destruction of Lot's deniers and salvation of believers show that God holds nations accountable; the preserved remains of their cities are a lesson for the fearful.
rows.anchor: These events bear witness historically that the Creator of this Universe takes account of what nations do

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh, ‘Ād, Thamūd, and Noah's people ignored their messengers and the law of retribution, then God destroyed them simply by commanding winds and clouds to unleash their terror.
rows.anchor: They were totally destroyed by the Almighty Who did not have to do much for this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing verses sum up that the Creator of the heavens, earth, and all paired things can recreate the world; people should turn toward God, while the Prophet should leave rebels and remind those who benefit.
rows.anchor: If the Day of Reckoning is certain to come, then people should run towards the Almighty and seek only His nearness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans and jinn were created to worship God, not to provide for others or sustain Him; He is the Provider and supports worshippers who serve Him through every circumstance.
rows.anchor: men and jinn have been created by Him only to worship Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wrongdoers will receive their appointed fate, but God grants respite until the truth is fully conveyed and no excuse to deny remains; then the warned Day arrives.
rows.anchor: they shall be given the respite needed so that the truth is communicated to them in its ultimate form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening waw is an oath; oaths by such things do not sanctify them but bear witness to a later or contextually evident claim, and waw can aptly be translated “bears witness.”
rows.anchor: the oaths which are sworn by such objects are not meant to sanctify these objects

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhāriyāt means winds that scatter dust; it functions as an adjective so conventional that it can replace the noun, while dharwan adds emphasis, rendered here by “fierce.”
rows.anchor: refers to winds which scatter dust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When fa links these adjectives, it marks sequence and makes them qualify the same noun; thus the next three descriptions refer to the winds.
rows.anchor: there is a sequence between them and secondly, these adjectives qualify the same noun

rows.speaker: those who regard them as adjectives of separate nouns
rows.claim: The author rejects the interpretation that each following adjective refers to a separate noun, since it violates the Arabic sequence rule and Qur'anic parallels.
rows.anchor: The opinion of those who have regarded them to be adjectives of separate nouns is against this rule

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parallel sequence in Sūrah al-‘Ādiyāt likewise describes galloping horses successively, supporting the reading that the Dhāriyāt adjectives share one referent.
rows.anchor: Panting, galloping horses bear witness which then
